strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: group-wise counterfactual attribution is formalized around the LOGO retraining target, and the observation that data removal is exactly the unlearning operation is a natural and useful framing that has not been directly exploited for group-level attribution in diffusion models.

The method is honest about its estimand: GUDA explicitly targets approximation of the LOGO counterfactual model and validates this approximation empirically against the oracle, rather than claiming deletion guarantees or conflating similarity with causal influence.

Useful theoretical grounding in Appendix A.1: the paper derives that ReTrack-style redirection is an unbiased reformulation of the retain-only (LOGO) training objective before truncation/fine-tuning approximations, giving a principled reason to prefer it over ad-hoc forget losses (supported by the ReTrack vs. ESD ablation: 72.7% vs. 61.9% top-1 on CIFAR-10).

Comprehensive experimental protocol: two settings (unconditional CIFAR-10, conditional UnlearnCanvas + SD 1.5), multiple head-focused metrics with clear justification, wall-clock time decomposition into preprocessing vs. query-time, hyperparameter ablations (epochs, λ, K, lr), and extensive implementation details in the appendix that support reproducibility.

Meaningful practical speedups: ~100× over LOGOA on CIFAR-10 and ~5× over LOGOA / ~18× over Wang et al. (2024) on UnlearnCanvas, with a sensible amortization argument (precomputed unlearned models, cheap query-time ELBO evaluation).

Careful experimental hygiene: exposure-matched training budgets between full and LOGO models, same timestep sampling and noise reuse across methods for ELBO computation, and evaluation prompts designed to prevent superficial prompt-cue exploitation.
weaknesses: Evaluation scale is limited. CIFAR-10 has only 10 well-separated classes, and the UnlearnCanvas experiment evaluates only 16 of 60 styles on a small stylized dataset (~24k images) explicitly constructed for unlearning evaluation. There is no evidence the approach scales to realistic-scale data (millions of images, many overlapping groups) or to large pretrained models beyond SD 1.5; the paper acknowledges overlapping groups as future work, but this is the practically important case.

Absolute attribution quality on the harder conditional benchmark is modest: 45.6% top-1 agreement, 0.239 Spearman, and Top-3 overlap of 0.405. While relative to baselines this is the best reported, the method still misidentifies the primary influencing style over half the time, limiting claims of practical usefulness for copyright/fair-compensation use cases motivating the paper.

Potential circularity in the evaluation: GUDA and LOGOA are both ELBO-difference scores, and GUDA's unlearning procedure is validated by agreement with an oracle that shares the same scoring rule. High agreement partly reflects score-rule compatibility rather than exclusively better counterfactual approximation; gradient-based methods forced into a different scoring pipeline (with ad-hoc aggregation) may be disadvantaged. The paper acknowledges this only implicitly ('rank-based metrics... less informative'), and does not analyze the decomposition.

The 'oracle' itself is a proxy: LOGOA is implemented by fine-tuning from the same SD 1.5 checkpoint rather than training on D_{-k} from scratch (for CIFAR-10, via a 'fine-tuning LOGO' proxy). Fidelity of this proxy to the true counterfactual is not itself quantified, so the reported agreement is fidelity to an approximation of the target.

Unlearning hyperparameters (e.g., 20 epochs, λ=0.03, lr) appear selected by their performance on the attribution metrics against the oracle (the shaded 'main configuration' is the best-performing one in ablation tables), raising a risk of tuning to the evaluation protocol; there are no confidence intervals or significance tests, and ELBO is estimated with only 100 timesteps and a single noise sample, so variance of the headline numbers is unknown.

The conditional GUDA-C method involves substantial hand-engineering (VLM-derived style descriptors, CLIP-weighted anchor selection, prompt synthesis templates), which is dataset-specific (requires structured style labels) and weakens generality; its theoretical connection to the LOGO conditional objective is looser than in the unconditional case.

No comparison to simpler counterfactual proxies (e.g., fine-tune-based LOGO with fewer steps, or influence-function group aggregates beyond D-TRAK/D-TRAK variants on UnlearnCanvas) that could contextualize the cost–accuracy tradeoff; Wang et al. (2024) is the only unlearning-based attribution baseline, and it is reimplemented rather than reproduced on identical footing.

strengths: The paper targets a genuinely important and underexplored problem: group-level (style/class) counterfactual attribution for diffusion models, where aggregating instance-level influence scores is known to be unreliable due to non-additivity. Framing group attribution as a data-removal query and connecting it to unlearning is a natural and sensible idea.

The CIFAR-10 experiment is well designed as a proof of concept: the LOGO oracle models are trained from scratch, the all-group model uses exposure-matched training (excluding one random class per epoch) to avoid confounding from different optimization budgets, and attribution is evaluated over 2,048 generated queries against a true counterfactual ground truth.

GUDA (ReTrack variant) outperforms semantic-similarity (CLIPA) and instance-level gradient methods (DAS, D-TRAK, TRAK) on most head-focused metrics, and GUDA w/ ESD provides a useful internal ablation showing that the choice of unlearning objective matters (72.7% vs 61.9% top-1).

The appendix is unusually thorough: derivation of ReTrack as an unbiased reformulation of the retain-only objective with clear discussion of the three practical approximations (k-NN truncation, finite fine-tuning, preservation regularizer), full hyperparameter tables, extensive ablations (epochs, lambda, K, learning rate), metric definitions, and wall-clock cost decompositions (preprocessing vs query-time).

Timing analysis is honest and informative, e.g., the speedup over LOGO is ~100x on CIFAR-10 but correctly reported as only ~5x on UnlearnCanvas, and the query-time/preprocessing amortization trade-off is analyzed explicitly.

The limitations and potential risks are discussed (overlap-free groups assumption, proxy oracle for large models, societal impacts), and the conditional-settable anchor construction (keep content, swap style via CLIP-weighted selection) is a reasonable practical contribution for the conditional setting where ReTrack's justification breaks down.
weaknesses: The fidelity of the unlearned model to the counterfactual target is only validated via ranking-agreement metrics, not by a direct statistical test that theta^ul_k matches theta^logo_k (e.g., distributional comparisons of generations, function-space distance, or KL divergence). Top-1 agreement of 72.7% (CIFAR-10) and Spearman of only 0.239-0.265 leave substantial unexplained discrepancy between the proposed proxy and the oracle, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for any comparison in Tables 1-2.

The flagship UnlearnCanvas experiment uses a weakened 'oracle': both the LOGO models and GUDA are fine-tuned from the same SD 1.5 checkpoint with the same recipe. This is disclosed, but it introduces a potential circularity - GUDA and the oracle share an initialization, training data pipeline, and optimization budget, which may inflate agreement independently of whether unlearning faithfully approximates true group-removal retraining. The headline claim that GUDA 'captures causal influence' is therefore supported most strongly only in the small-scale CIFAR-10 setting.

Scalability claims are overstated relative to the actual method: GUDA still requires N unlearning runs (one per group), so preprocessing cost remains O(N) in the number of groups, exactly the bottleneck the paper motivates against for LOGO. The savings come only from fewer steps per group (~1/120 of retraining on CIFAR-10, ~1/5 on UnlearnCanvas), and the 5x speedup on the realistic setting is far from the headline ~100x.

The conditional instantiation (GUDA-C) is largely heuristic: anchor construction via CLIP-weighted style-descriptor swapping has no theoretical connection to the LOGO objective (unlike GUDA-U), depends on descriptor extraction from a VLM (Qwen2.5-VL), and its quality is not ablated (e.g., sensitivity to tau, eta_mix, or the descriptor vocabulary is not studied).

Several baselines perform near-randomly (TRAK at 11.8% top-1 vs 10% chance on CIFAR-10; Wang et al. at 4.7% vs 6.25% chance on UnlearnCanvas). While the authors report hyperparameter sweeps, such extreme failures raise concerns about the fairness of the baseline comparisons, and the strong conclusions against gradient-based methods rest on these implementations.

Absolute head-identification performance in the realistic setting is modest (45.6% top-1 of 16 classes on UnlearnCanvas, 320 queries only), and the evaluation covers a restricted, alphabetically-selected 16-style subset of 60 styles, which limits the evidence that the method works at the scale practitioners would need (the paper itself notes the group-partition and large-N settings as open problems).

The technical novelty is limited: the core unconditional mechanism is ReTrack applied as a computational proxy with a standard distillation preservation term, and the ELBO-difference scoring rule is borrowed from prior work; the contribution is primarily an empirical framework and evaluation protocol rather than a new method or new theoretical understanding. The ELBO surrogate also remains latent-space-only for LDMs (VAE likelihood omitted), which the paper acknowledges but does not quantify the impact of.

strengths: The problem formulation is clear and well-motivated: group-wise counterfactual attribution (what would change if a group were absent from training?) is a practically relevant question that instance-level methods (TRAK, D-TRAK, D-TRAK) do not directly answer, and the paper clearly distinguishes this estimand from instance-level attribution.

The core idea — using machine unlearning as a computational approximation to Leave-One-Group-Out retraining — is natural and well-executed, and the paper is appropriately careful that unlearning is used as an approximation tool, not as a certified deletion mechanism.

Appendix A.1 provides a genuinely useful theoretical justification: ReTrack's redirection objective is derived as an unbiased reformulation of the retain-only (LOGO) training objective before practical truncations, which explains why the ReTrack forget loss outperforms ESD in the experiments (72.7% vs 61.9% top-1 on CIFAR-10) rather than being an ad-hoc choice.

The evaluation is validated against LOGO oracle counterfactuals in two settings (CIFAR-10 classes and UnlearnCanvas styles with SD 1.5), including a controlled prompt-shift design on UnlearnCanvas that deliberately avoids label leakage through training prompts — a thoughtful evaluation detail.

Reproducibility is strong: the appendix provides full hyperparameters, ablations over epochs/λ/K/learning rate (Tables 4–7), baseline reimplementation details, prompt construction, timing breakdowns, and an explicit discussion of loss-weighting conventions across the two experimental settings.

The paper is honest about approximation deviations (K-NN truncation, preservation regularizer introducing controlled bias), the weak full-ranking Spearman correlations, and why head-focused metrics are emphasized; limitations around group definitions (non-overlapping groups) and fairness are acknowledged in the Impact Statement.
weaknesses: The 'oracle' in the large-scale setting is not actual LOGO retraining: for UnlearnCanvas, both the all-group model and the LOGO models are fine-tuned from the same SD 1.5 checkpoint. This makes the counterfactual target a fine-tuning proxy, so the central claim of approximating 'the counterfactual model trained without group k' is validated only against this proxy, and its gap to true from-scratch retraining at scale is unquantified.

Hyperparameters for GUDA (unlearning epochs, λ, K, learning rate, τ, ηmix) are selected by sweeping against LOGOA agreement on the same evaluation protocol used for the headline results (Tables 4–7 and Appendix B.1), creating a risk of benchmark overfitting; no held-out validation split or error bars/seed variance are reported for the main comparisons.

Scale is limited: experiments cover 10 CIFAR-10 classes and 16 of 60 UnlearnCanvas styles. Since GUDA's preprocessing scales linearly with the number of groups (one unlearned model per group), scalability to realistically large group counts (e.g., thousands of artists) is asserted but not demonstrated.

Full-ranking quality is weak (Spearman ≈ 0.24–0.27 across settings), meaning GUDA is reliable mainly for head identification; the paper argues this reflects tail irrelevance, but applications like fair compensation over many contributors may need tail fidelity, so the practical scope is narrower than the framing suggests.

The scoring rule itself (ELBO difference) is a surrogate for log-likelihood, and in the SD setting ELBO is computed in latent space only (no VAE likelihood term); the paper acknowledges ELBO need not preserve likelihood ordering, so attribution quality partly depends on the surrogate's fidelity, which is not independently analyzed.

GUDA-C's anchor construction (CLIP-weighted style selection plus prompt synthesis via descriptor surgery) is heuristic and involves several tuned components; sensitivity of the conditional results to these design choices beyond the small τ/ηmix sweep is unclear.

Some baselines underperform expectations (D-TRAK at 60.9%, TRAK near-random at 11.8% top-1), which may partly reflect adaptation difficulties of instance-level methods to this setting; stronger tuning or additional group-aggregation baselines would strengthen the claim that direct counterfactual targeting is superior.

strengths: The paper formalizes a clear and well-motivated estimand (LOGOA) for group-wise attribution as an ELBO difference between the full-data model and a leave-one-group-out counterfactual, and the unlearning-based approximation (GUDA) directly targets this quantity rather than aggregating instance-level scores or using similarity proxies.

The empirical validation against the LOGO oracle is unusually thorough and honest: the authors transparently disclose that their 'oracle' is a fine-tuning LOGO proxy for large models, validate the ELBO surrogate against a PF-ODE likelihood oracle (Appendix D.5, showing Pearson 0.820 and stable head identification), and include ablations (anchor strategy, ReTrack hyperparameters, DAS aggregation), a noisy-partition robustness check, and detailed wall-clock cost decomposition.

The evaluation covers two settings spanning practical difficulty (unconditional CIFAR-10 classes and conditional SD 1.5 style attribution with deliberately shifted evaluation prompts), and GUDA achieves the best or tied-best head-focused metrics (Top-1, MRR, NDCG@3, RBO) against reasonable baselines (CLIPA, DAS, D-TRAK, TRAK, Wang et al.), with ~100x speedup over LOGO retraining on CIFAR-10 and ~5x on UnlearnCanvas.

The conditional extension (GUDA-C) thoughtfully identifies a real failure mode of naive conditional ReTrack extension (condition-distribution mismatch when a style group is removed) and the AWSS anchor design is ablated against simpler alternatives.

Limitations (ELBO KL-gap asymmetry, no approximation-error bound for the truncated ReTrack objective, disjoint group assumption, non-additivity, scope of evaluation) are candidly discussed in Appendix E, and the impact statement correctly notes the unlearning operator is not a certified deletion mechanism.
weaknesses: Margins over the strongest baseline are modest and no statistical significance is reported: on CIFAR-10 GUDA's Top-1 (0.727) is only ~1 point above DAS (0.716), and DAS matches or exceeds GUDA on Spearman and Top-3 under the stricter likelihood oracle (Table 13b); attribution metrics are computed from a single set of models/runs with no error bars or seed variance, so the headline claim that GUDA 'identifies primary contributing groups more reliably' than DAS is weaker than presented.

Scalability claims are overstated in one direction: GUDA still requires one unlearning run per group during preprocessing, so cost grows linearly in the number of groups (the same N+1 scaling as LOGOA, just with a much smaller constant); the practical regime where this wins is large query sets, and the paper evaluates only 10 and 16 groups, leaving behavior with hundreds/thousands of groups untested.

Theoretical support is asymmetric: the unconditional case benefits from the ReTrack importance-sampling derivation (Appendix A.1), but the conditional case (GUDA-C) rests on a heuristic anchor-redirection design with no formal connection to the conditional LOGO objective, and no theoretical argument that the ELBO-difference score under an unlearned model approximates the LOGOA score other than empirical correlation on CIFAR-10.

The central premise that unlearning artifacts do not contaminate the attribution signal (i.e., that the ELBO gap of an unlearned model reflects removed group influence rather than optimization side effects of unlearning) is only validated in a small-group, small-model regime; on UnlearnCanvas the fidelity of GUDA-C to LOGOA is assumed rather than decomposed (e.g., no comparison of unlearned-model generations against LOGO-model generations analogous to the CIFAR-10 Figure 3).

Experimental scope is limited (CIFAR-10 and 16 of 60 UnlearnCanvas styles on SD 1.5), and the code availability statement in the abstract is incomplete (no URL), which together reduce reproducibility and the ability to judge generalization to larger models and more group definitions.

strengths: Clear and careful problem formalization: the paper defines an explicit group-removal counterfactual estimand (LOGOA) with LOGO retraining as an oracle, which is a more principled target than similarity or additive instance-level scores, and the distinction between instance-level and group-level attribution is well argued.

Unusually thorough empirical validation for this kind of method: comparisons against multiple baselines (CLIPA, DAS, D-TRAK, TRAK, Wang et al.), ablations over every major hyperparameter (epochs, λ, K, learning rate, anchor strategy), a PF-ODE likelihood-oracle cross-check of the ELBO proxy (D.5), a noisy-partition robustness study (D.6), and detailed wall-clock cost accounting.

Honest limitations section (Appendix E) that correctly identifies the ELBO ordering problem, the uncontrolled bias of the truncated ReTrack operator, and the disjoint-partition assumption; the impact statement also explicitly disclaims deletion guarantees.

The conditional anchor construction (GUDA-C, keep-content/swap-style) is a thoughtful response to a real condition-distribution mismatch problem, and the ablation in Table 3 supports each design choice.
weaknesses: Potential evaluation-oracle bias undermines the headline claims. GUDA and the LOGOA 'gold standard' share the exact same scoring rule (∆ELBO with the same timestep grid and reused noise), and the unlearning procedure distills toward θ_full on the retain set, shaping the very ELBO behavior used for scoring. A method evaluated under the same surrogate it implicitly optimizes toward is structurally favored. The PF-ODE check in D.5 partially mitigates this, but under the likelihood oracle GUDA's margin over DAS shrinks to 0.645 vs 0.639 Top-1, and DAS overtakes GUDA on NDCG@3, Top-3, and Spearman — suggesting the reported advantages are partly an artifact of the ELBO oracle choice.

No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals anywhere. With only 320 UnlearnCanvas queries and 16 styles, and margins over CLIPA/DAS of a few percentage points (e.g., 0.456 vs 0.338 Top-1 is meaningful, but 0.727 vs 0.716 vs CLIPA 0.662 on CIFAR-10 is not clearly separated), the reader cannot judge whether differences are stable.

The 'gold standard' is itself weakened on the flagship benchmark: the UnlearnCanvas LOGO oracle is a fine-tuning proxy from the same SD 1.5 checkpoint rather than true retraining, so both the oracle and GUDA are fine-tuned variants of θ_full, and only 16 of 60 styles are evaluated. This makes the oracle-vs-approximation framing less convincing than it first appears.

Modest methodological novelty: the unconditional instantiation is essentially 'apply existing ReTrack unlearning (Shi et al., 2026) and take ELBO differences,' and the conditional variant is an engineering extension. The paper is candid that the unlearning operator is not new, but the remaining contribution (the estimand + validation) is a relatively thin delta over Choi et al. (2025) and Wang et al. (2024), who already connect unlearning to attribution.

Scalability claims are overstated relative to evidence: GUDA requires one unlearned model per group, so cost grows linearly in the number of groups and everything must be recomputed if groups or the model change. Experiments cover at most 60 groups on a single curated, style-disjoint benchmark; real group structures (many artists, overlapping concepts) are untested, and the disjoint-partition assumption is acknowledged but only lightly stress-tested.

The strongest empirical gaps are against baselines that appear weakly tuned for the setting (TRAK at near-chance Top-1; Wang et al. at 4.7% Top-1), while the genuinely competitive baseline (CLIPA) costs essentially nothing (<1 minute) — narrowing the practical significance of GUDA's improvement.

strengths: The paper formalizes a clear and well-motivated estimand (LOGOA: per-generation group influence as an ELBO difference against a LOGO counterfactual model), and the framing of machine unlearning as a computational approximation of a counterfactual model — rather than a deletion mechanism — is a genuinely useful conceptual bridge between the attribution and unlearning literatures.

Validation against the oracle is unusually thorough: the authors actually retrain LOGO counterfactual models (10 on CIFAR-10, 16 on UnlearnCanvas with SD 1.5) and evaluate agreement with LOGOA using multiple head-focused and full-ranking metrics, rather than relying on proxy ground truth alone.

The ELBO-as-likelihood-surrogate concern is addressed empirically (Appendix D.5): the authors build a PF-ODE likelihood oracle, report Pearson/Spearman correlation between ΔELBO and Δlog p, and re-evaluate all methods under the likelihood oracle, honestly noting where DAS/D-TRAK become more competitive on broader ranking metrics.

Extensive ablations cover the design space: unlearning operator choice (ReTrack vs. ESD), anchor strategy (AWSS vs. uniform vs. style-removed), hyperparameters (epochs, λ, K, lr), baseline aggregation strategies and regularization sweeps, and robustness to 5% noisy group partitions.

Wall-clock timing is decomposed into preprocessing vs. query time with amortization analysis (Tabs. 11–12, App. D.3–D.4), which is the right way to assess practicality, and the paper is candid that the speedup over fine-tuning-based LOGO is ~5.2× on UnlearnCanvas versus the ~100× headline figure on CIFAR-10.

The conditional extension (GUDA-C) tackles a real difficulty — prompt distribution shift when removing a style group — with a principled diagnosis (ReTrack's posterior target is ill-defined for out-of-support forget conditions) and an empirically validated remedy.

Limitations, ethics/impact, and non-deployment caveats (no certified deletion guarantees) are discussed honestly, and experimental details in the appendix (hyperparameters, prompts, protocols, code link) support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Experimental scope is narrow: only 10 groups (CIFAR-10) and 16 styles (UnlearnCanvas, first 16 alphabetically). Since GUDA's preprocessing scales linearly with the number of groups (one unlearning run per group), the practicality claims for 'scaling to many groups' (Sec. 4.3, D.3) are not demonstrated at group counts where the linear cost would become a concern.

Margins over the strongest baselines are thin and metric-dependent: on CIFAR-10, GUDA's Top-1 (0.727) is only ~1 point above DAS (0.716), DAS actually edges GUDA on Spearman (0.267 vs. 0.265), and under the likelihood oracle DAS and D-TRAK become more competitive on NDCG@3/Top-3/Spearman (Tab. 13b). The claimed superiority holds mainly for head identification, and no statistical significance or error bars over repeated runs are reported.

Absolute attribution quality is moderate: 45.6% Top-1 and Spearman ~0.24 on UnlearnCanvas, and full-ranking agreement is weak across all settings — the paper acknowledges this but it limits how far the method can be reliably used beyond head identification.

The UnlearnCanvas 'oracle' is not true retraining: LOGO models are fine-tuned from the same SD 1.5 checkpoint as the full model. While disclosed and framed as standard practice, this weakens the counterfactual gold standard precisely in the more realistic text-to-image setting, and both the oracle and GUDA share the same ELBO scoring rule, so some evaluation advantage for GUDA-family methods cannot be fully excluded (partially mitigated by the D.5 likelihood-oracle check, which is CIFAR-10 only).

Theoretical grounding is largely inherited: the unconditional case borrows ReTrack's unbiasedness argument, and the practical loss deviates from it (density-ratio omission, K-NN truncation, distillation preservation term) with no formal error bound; the conditional anchor design (AWSS) is heuristic and validated only empirically.

Key experimental details such as the number of random seeds for model training/unlearning and variance of the reported metrics are not stated, which matters given that differences between top methods are small.

The abstract's '~100× speedup' claim derives from the smallest-scale, from-scratch-LOGO setting; the more realistic large-model comparison is ~5×, and the abstract's framing could overstate practical gains for large models.
